analysis.one_liner: Cuts acid rain pollution from coal plants and raises automobile fuel-economy standards.
analysis.headline: Introduced in January 1989 with a single cosponsor, the bill sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never received a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required a 12-million-ton reduction in sulfur dioxide emissions by 2000, forcing high-sulfur coal plants to clean their coal and set state-by-state emissions cuts, while tightening nitrogen oxide limits. It also would have raised fuel-economy standards for cars and light trucks by up to 65 percent over their 1988 levels, increased the tax on gas-guzzling vehicles, and offered tax credits for efficient cars. Compliance costs would have been partially offset by a small fee on electricity generation that funded subsidies for pollution-control equipment.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of regions damaged by acid rain (lakes, forests, and ecosystems in the Northeast and elsewhere), people breathing coal-plant pollution downwind, and drivers who would save on fuel as vehicle efficiency rose; the bill also aimed to reduce oil imports and greenhouse gas emissions.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a reduction of 12 million tons of sulfur dioxide emissions per year and 3 million tons of nitrogen oxides by 2000 to lessen damage to public health and the environment from acid deposition.

Forces plants burning coal with more than 2 percent sulfur to clean that coal before combustion, and requires plants with smokestack scrubbers to add adipic acid treatment to make them work better, both by the end of 1990.

Divides the emissions cuts among the 48 contiguous states by formula, lets states choose how to get there, and applies a federal emissions limit to sources in any state that fails to submit or implement an approved plan.
Raises average fuel-economy standards for passenger cars and light trucks in steps of 20, 45, and 65 percent above each manufacturer's 1988 performance, with the largest increases by model year 2000.
Raises the 'gas guzzler' tax on inefficient new cars and creates tax credits of up to $2,000 for buyers of unusually fuel-efficient vehicles.

Sets up an Acid Deposition Control Fund, financed by a fee of 0.5 to 1.6 mills per kilowatt-hour on fossil-fuel electricity, to pay utilities $147 per ton of pollution cut for 15 years and to fund state programs restoring waters damaged by acid rain.

analysis.who_pays: Electric utilities burning high-sulfur coal and their customers, who would bear compliance costs and a generation fee only partially offset by subsidies; high-sulfur coal producers facing cleaning requirements and possible job losses; and automakers facing steep fuel-economy targets and higher taxes on inefficient models.

drawbacks.text: The bill itself puts a fee on every kilowatt-hour of electricity generated by fossil-fuel plants, which utilities would pass through to customers, and the $147-per-ton subsidies it offers come from that same fee pool rather than new money.
The bill acknowledges the risk of 'coal mining job dislocation' and subsidizes control-technology capital costs to blunt it, an admission that high-sulfur coal regions would bear real economic costs.

The fuel-economy targets—up to 65 percent above each manufacturer's 1988 fleet average by 2000—were aggressive; the bill lets manufacturers seek modifications capped at half a mile per gallon and requires an economic-justification review, reflecting concerns about feasibility and cost.

The design is prescriptive: federally mandated coal cleaning, fixed state-by-state tonnage shares, and a uniform 1.0 pound-per-million-Btu emissions limit, rather than the flexible market-based allowance trading that Congress ultimately adopted in 1990 (a general point about how the policy landscape moved on, not a claim from the bill itself).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The environmental and public-health goals were real and the bill tried to soften the blow on coal regions and ratepayers with subsidies and a state-flexibility structure. But it was a rigid, command-driven design with costs concentrated on coal-dependent utilities, mining jobs, and electricity customers, and its automotive targets were far more ambitious than anything then in force. Its core objective was nonetheless achieved a year later by the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments, using a more flexible approach.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and never came out; no committee vote, no floor vote, nothing further through the end of the 101st Congress.

narrative.text: Senator John Kerry, joined by Senator Edward Kennedy, introduced the National Acid Rain Control Act of 1989 on January 25, 1989.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
No further action of any kind appears in the record for the remainder of the 101st Congress, which ended January 3, 1991.
The bill never advanced beyond introduction; its only cosponsor was Senator Kennedy.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electric utilities and high-sulfur coal interests avoided this bill's mandated cuts, coal-cleaning requirements, and generation fee for another two years. The public did not lose the policy for long, because Congress enacted acid rain controls with a different design in the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments, but under this bill's timeline those reductions would have started years earlier.

for.name: John F. Kerry
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; bill's lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut acid rain pollution and raise fuel-economy standards.

for.name: Edward M. Kennedy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; sole cosponsor

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

against.name: High-sulfur coal and coal-fired utility interests
against.role: Industries in the Midwest and Appalachia that would bear the bill's costs
against.what_they_did: Opposed acid rain control legislation during this period, arguing cleanup costs and coal job losses.

against.name: President George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Proposed his own acid rain control plan in 1989, which became the basis for the acid rain title of the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments rather than this bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan split was never revealed; the bill had two Democratic sponsors from Massachusetts and no recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed coal-cleaning mandates, a 1.0 pound-per-million-Btu emissions limit, and a fee on every kilowatt-hour generated, but it also paid utilities $147 per ton of pollution reduced for 15 years out of that fee fund and required that subsidies lower customers' bills. The industry's interest in stopping the bill ran against the public's interest in cleaner air.

Plants burning coal with more than 2 percent sulfur would have had to clean it before combustion, and the bill concedes the risk of coal mining job dislocation, offering subsidies to cushion it. Cheaper compliance options like fuel switching would shift demand toward low-sulfur coal.

The bill would have raised fuel-economy requirements up to 65 percent above 1988 fleet averages by model year 2000, extended standards to light trucks, tightened nitrogen oxide limits, and increased gas-guzzler taxes, offset only partly by credits for efficient vehicles and a modification process.

industries.industry: Low-sulfur coal producers and pollution-control equipment makers
industries.note: Coal cleaning requirements, fuel-switching options, and subsidized scrubber upgrades would have created demand for cleaner coal and control technology.
